rv.q: “The Verge,” directed by Jessie Austrian at the Public Theater, frequently refers to characters’ being “queer,” although in 1921, the word still mostly meant “strange.” Glaspell may not have been overtly (or consciously) referring to same-sex relationships, yet straight sexuality is certainly depicted as explicitly deranging.
The great danger, though, and one that fully manifests here, is that speechifying like Claire’s slams up against the fourth wall and ricochets back at her.
Silverman’s Claire is a shot to the heart.
It's been a very long time since I actually gasped during a performance, but gasp I did with this one all the way through to its tormented ending.
Based on the dark poetry and feminist verve of The Verge , Glaspell’s oeuvre is one worth rediscovering.

Ultimately the verbose, symbol-coded play scarcely proves to be a lost masterpiece, but offers great interest to scholars of course, and it’s a little late in the day anyway to criticize Glaspell’s dramaturgy.

Susan Glaspell’s 1921 play is a fascinating feminist text that offers fresh insights on the experience of patriarchal oppression, but The Verge is perhaps too cerebral for some audience members to fully enjoy it in performance.

Getting tangled up in The Verge is a highly enjoyable adventure for those open to the idea that it is healthy for a woman to want more from her life, even if the ways she goes about it seem obsessive and odd.
This is a problematic show with all-too-rare flashes of genius and ahead-of-its-time perspectives.

cn.t: Mixed reviews for Fiasco Theater's revival of Glaspell's century-old drama, with critics split on whether this rediscovered feminist work remains compellingly strange or just too talky and obscure for modern audiences.
